name: LP3982ILD-ADJ_NOPB
title: 300 mA low-noise CMOS LDO regulator with shutdown and fault flag
summary: The LP3982 is a 300 mA linear regulator with a PMOS pass device, running from 2.5 V to 6 V in. It comes as fixed 1.8, 2.5, 2.82, 3.0 and 3.3 V versions and an adjustable version (1.25 V to 6 V, set by two resistors on SET), in an 8-pin VSSOP or an 8-pin 2.5 mm × 3 mm WSON with exposed pad. Dropout is 120 mV typical at 300 mA, ground current 90 µA typical with no load, and shutdown current 1 nA typical. A capacitor on CC lowers output noise to 37 µVRMS; an open-drain FAULT output flags current limit, thermal shutdown and approaching dropout. Its pinout, package and specification match the MAX8860.

circuits.title: Typical application (fixed VOUT version)
circuits.description: A fixed-voltage LP3982 with 2.2 µF on the input and 2.2 µF ceramic on the output. SHDN is tied to IN so the regulator is always on. A 100 kΩ resistor from OUT pulls up the open-drain FAULT line, which leaves the circuit as a flag. 33 nF from CC to ground is the noise bypass. SET is unused in the fixed versions.

circuits.title: Minimum battery detector that disconnects the load through SHDN
circuits.description: A four-cell NiMH battery (VB) feeds the LP3982 and an LMC7215 comparator. An LM385 1.2 V reference, biased from VB through 180 kΩ, sits on the comparator's inverting input. The non-inverting input watches VB through the divider R1 768 kΩ over R3 301 kΩ, and R2 2.74 MΩ from the comparator output back to that node adds hysteresis. The comparator output drives SHDN: when VB falls to the lower threshold, 3.6 V, the regulator turns off and drops the load; it turns on again only once the resting battery recovers above the upper threshold, 4.6 V. The output has 2.2 µF ceramic and a 100 kΩ pull-up on FAULT.
notes: The comparator must be rail-to-rail at both its inputs and its output.
The resistor values are the nearest practical values to those from the threshold equations, with GT = 5 µmho.

circuits.title: Power-on delayed reset
circuits.description: The LP3982 runs with SHDN tied to IN and a 3 V output. FAULT is pulled up to the output by RP, 100 kΩ, and loaded by CDELAY, 0.1 µF, so after a fault clears the FAULT node ramps up slowly. An LMC7225 comparator, supplied from the output, compares that ramp with the bandgap voltage on CC and holds a microprocessor's active-low RESET until the ramp passes it; the delay set this way is 8.8 ms. The comparator output has its own pull-up to the 3 V rail. Its inputs must be high impedance so that they do not load the reference on CC.

equations.name: Loop gain model
equations.expr: LG(jω) = [AO / (1 + jω/ωPOLE)] × [(1 + jω × ESR × CL) / (1 + jω × (ESR + RO ∥ RL) × CL)]
equations.note: The first factor is the error amplifier: gain and one pole. The second is the load: a zero from ESR and CL, and a pole from CL with ESR plus RO in parallel with RL. With a low-ESR ceramic the load zero sits at too high a frequency to offset the load pole, so the LP3982 places an internal zero near unity gain to keep phase margin.

operation.text: The loop is a 1.25 V bandgap reference driving an error amplifier that controls a PMOS pass device, with feedback from the output through R1 and R2 to the amplifier. The divider is inside the fixed versions and outside, on SET, in the adjustable version. Shutdown, fault comparators, current limit and thermal protection surround it. The PMOS pass device draws almost no drive current, unlike a PNP pass device.
Pinout, package and performance match the MAX8860, except that the LP3982 has no reverse-battery protection and no combined fixed/adjustable dual mode.
The regulator stays stable with no load at all, as needed for keeping CMOS RAM alive.

An internal 500 µA source charges the CC capacitor until it is near 90 % of its final voltage, so the noise bypass capacitor does not slow start-up much. Start-up to 90 % of VOUT is 120 µs typical with 10 µF output. A smaller CC gives faster turn-on.

SHDN low (0.4 V max) puts the part to sleep: the bandgap, error amplifier and pass transistor switch off and supply current falls to 1 nA typical. SHDN at 2 V or more turns it on. SHDN may be tied straight to VIN for always-on use, and may go above VIN as long as it stays at or below 6.5 V.

The adjustable version behaves as a non-inverting amplifier of the 1.25 V reference, with a gain of 1 + R1/R2, whose output transistor can only source current. R1 runs from OUT to SET and R2 from SET to ground; R2 = 100 kΩ is the recommended value. The output sits on the pass device drain, so it can come close to the input, at the cost of a high output impedance that needs some series resistance with the load capacitance; the output capacitor's own ESR usually supplies it.

Ceramic output capacitors down to 2.2 µF are supported. Larger values and other types also work if their ESR stays below 0.5 Ω. Of the ceramic dielectrics, Z5U and Y5V can lose half their capacitance or more as they warm from 25 °C, X5R generally holds within ±20 %, and X7R within 10 % over temperature. Because a ceramic's ESR zero is too high in frequency to compensate the load pole, the LP3982 generates its own internal zero to keep the loop stable.

About 1 µF minimum is needed at the input, and more is fine; its type does not matter for stability. With long supply leads on a bench, especially near dropout and at high current, the lead inductance can couple through the pass transistor's gate oxide into the loop and cause instability; a 10 µF tantalum at the input damps it. A 1 µF ceramic is enough in most finished designs. Tantalum capacitors can fail short, which could damage the part.

CC, from pin 6 to ground, lowers output noise markedly; 33 nF is the optimum. Pin 6 is the high-impedance bandgap output, so capacitor leakage loads the reference and pulls the output voltage down: NPO/C0G ceramics leak very little, and polypropylene or polycarbonate film parts even less. CC does not change the load transient response but lengthens turn-on time.

FAULT goes low in current limit, in thermal shutdown, and when the input-to-output difference falls toward dropout. The dropout comparison uses a threshold a little above the dropout voltage that follows the dropout as load current changes. FAULT is open drain and needs a pull-up of high value to save power; 100 kΩ suits most uses.

On the WSON the main heat path is the exposed pad, joined by vias to a buried ground plane of adequate copper area. On the VSSOP heat leaves through the pins. Thermal shutdown turns the pass transistor off at about 160 °C junction and back on about 10 °C lower. The listed RθJA is for the JESD51-7 board and serves only to compare packages; on a well laid-out board RθJA is RθJC(bot) plus whatever the board copper adds as heat spreader. Higher input-to-output headroom costs dissipation but improves PSRR and transient behaviour.
The input supply should be well regulated, between 2.5 V and 6 V. If it is noisy, extra low-ESR input capacitance improves output noise.

Mount CIN, COUT and CCC close to the package, on the board face that carries the LP3982. Return the CIN and COUT grounds to the GND pin with short, wide copper. Long, narrow traces add inductance and resistance that hurt transient behaviour. In the WSON adjustable layout example, COUT sits beside OUT (pin 1) and CIN beside IN and GND (pins 2 and 3) with vias to the ground layer, the FAULT pull-up goes from pin 8 to a via on VOUT, CCC sits at CC (pin 6), and R1 and R2 sit next to SET (pin 5).

Use non-solder-mask-defined (NSMD) pads, extended 0.2 mm beyond each package terminal so that a solder fillet forms for reliability and inspection. How well heat leaves depends on the board stack and on copper area tied to the DAP. Conductive die-attach adhesive bonds the DAP to the die substrate, and has no wire to any pin; a parasitic PN junction lies between substrate and device ground. Connect the DAP to ground at pin 3. Leaving it floating is possible but not recommended, and it must not be tied to any net but ground.
